<!-- The prompt for a review-loop round. `.github/workflows/review-loop.yml` fills in
the braced names and passes the result to the reviewer. {PASS} is empty, except on an
Opus round that follows rounds by another reviewer (`OPUS_LATE` in the renderer). -->
Review pull request #{PR} in {REPOSITORY}.
This is review round {ROUND}. Your verdict decides
whether the closing comment asks for another round; the implementer adds
one otherwise only if its fixes grow beyond what you described. An agent can
ask for at most {MAX_ROUNDS} rounds — which is the
skill's own round budget (its §4), so review as it tells you to and let the
verdict say whether another round is needed rather than padding one to
reach it.
{PASS}
Follow this repository's own review skill, in full, as if it had been invoked
by name: read `.claude/skills/code-review-skill/SKILL.md` first, then the one
reference doc its §1 names for this kind of review, and obey them over any
generic review habit. In particular:

- The three-block output shape (§3), stable finding IDs kept across rounds,
  and §6 for posting: inline review comments for located findings, blocks 1
  and 3 in the review body, `event: COMMENT`.
- Open every comment you post with a heading, per §6: the round and the
  verdict on the review body, the ID with its severity and confidence on an
  inline finding. Post no table in anything — bullets instead.
- On any round after the first, open with one status bullet per previous ID
  before any new finding.
- Do not re-run the gates. Do not edit any code. You are reviewing.
- The project is installed (`python` is its environment), so measure a
  claim when you can rather than only reading the code.
- Do not write a prompt or brief for whoever fixes this. They read the PR.

How to work, which decides what the round costs: every turn re-sends the whole
context. Send independent tool calls together in one turn (a diff stat, a grep
and two file reads whose outputs do not depend on each other go out as one
message); make a call alone only when its output decides the next one. Send
reading of source and tests the diff does not touch to `Task` subagents with
`model: "sonnet"`, several in parallel. Ask a subagent what the code does, not
to confirm a suspicion, and for `file:line` facts with the lines that show them
and what it looked for and did not find. Re-read the lines a finding cites before
you file it: a subagent's summary is a lead, not evidence. Read yourself the diff
and the review's own instructions and contracts (the skill, its reference doc,
`CONTRIBUTING.md`, the specs and design notes): SKILL.md §How to spend turns.

Use `gh` for GitHub writes. End every comment you post with a `---` rule and
`_Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code)_`.

Then write `/tmp/loop-verdict.json`, and nothing else to that path:

{
  "verdict": "clean" | "approved" | "conditional" | "findings" | "decision",
  "summary": "at most 400 characters, plain language, no finding IDs and no
              file paths: what someone who has not opened the diff needs to
              know about where this PR stands",
  "question": "if verdict is decision: the one question for the maintainer,
               in plain language, answerable in a word or a short line.
               Otherwise an empty string"
}

`verdict` is "decision" if block 3 has anything in it at all — a maintainer
decision stops the review, and that beats the findings. It is "clean" only
if block 2 is empty.

Otherwise it carries your verdict line (§4), and this is the field that decides
whether another round is asked for, so match it to what you actually wrote:

- "approved" for a plain ✅ Approve: nothing is left for the implementer to
  fix. ("clean" is narrower: block 2 empty, so a plain ✅ Approve over
  💡/📚/🎉 annotations is "approved", not "clean".)
- "conditional" for ✅ Approve conditional on the listed fixes, and for
  💬 Comment: the findings are the implementer's to fix, and you do not need
  to see the result.

  Neither asks for another round; the findings are still posted in full and
  the implementer still works through them. The two differ only in the
  label the pull request is left with, so pick the one that matches your
  verdict line.
- "findings" for 🔄 Request Changes — a 🔴 stands, or a fix wants a look once
  it lands. That is what asks for the next round.

Pick "findings" only when you need to see the fixes, not to be safe: if what
is left is small and you have said exactly what to change (a wording fix, a
renamed test), a whole round spent checking that it was done is the waste the
round cap is there to stop. The other way round, never write "approved" or
"conditional" while a 🔴 is still open.
